clinicalPearls: ARF is a multisystem autoimmune sequela of group A streptococcal infection; almost all manifestations resolve completely, the major exception being cardiac valvular damage (rheumatic heart disease, RHD), which may persist after other features disappear (Harrison 22e p.2854).

Mainly a disease of children aged 5-14 years; initial episodes are rare in persons aged >30 years, whereas recurrent episodes remain relatively common in adolescents and young adults. RHD prevalence peaks between 25 and 40 years (Harrison 22e p.2854).
There is no clear gender association for ARF, but RHD more commonly affects females, sometimes up to twice as often as males (Harrison 22e p.2854).

Latent period of ~3 weeks (range 1-5 weeks) between the precipitating group A streptococcal infection and onset of ARF; the exceptions are chorea and indolent (low-grade) carditis, which may follow prolonged latent periods of up to 6 months (Harrison 22e p.2855).

Most common clinical features are polyarthritis (60-75% of cases) and carditis (50-75%); chorea prevalence varies from <2% to 30% between populations; erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules are now rare, found in <5% of cases (Harrison 22e p.2855).

Up to 75% of patients with ARF progress to RHD; the mitral valve is almost always affected, sometimes with the aortic valve. Isolated aortic valve involvement is rare. The characteristic manifestation of carditis in previously unaffected individuals is mitral regurgitation, sometimes with aortic regurgitation (Harrison 22e p.2855).

ARF arthritis is typically a migratory polyarthritis of large joints (knees, ankles, hips, elbows), asymmetric, severe and disabling, and highly responsive to salicylates/NSAIDs (Harrison 22e p.2855-2856).

Sydenham's chorea often occurs in the absence of other manifestations, follows a prolonged latent period, and is found mainly in females; more than 50% of patients presenting with chorea will have carditis, so echocardiography should be part of the workup (Harrison 22e p.2856).

Erythema marginatum is an evanescent serpiginous rash (pink macules clearing centrally) usually on the trunk, sometimes the limbs, but almost never on the face. Subcutaneous nodules are painless, mobile, occur over bony prominences, appear 2-3 weeks after onset, and are commonly associated with carditis (Harrison 22e p.2856).

Revised Jones criteria (2015 AHA): for all populations with evidence of preceding group A strep infection, initial ARF requires 2 major OR 1 major plus 2 minor manifestations; recurrent ARF requires 2 major OR 1 major plus 2 minor OR 3 minor manifestations. Separate, more sensitive criteria apply to moderate/high-risk populations versus low-risk populations (Harrison 22e p.2856-2857).

Major manifestations: carditis (clinical and/or subclinical), arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules; in moderate/high-risk populations arthritis includes monoarthritis and polyarthralgia (Harrison 22e p.2857).

Secondary prevention with long-term penicillin prophylaxis is the mainstay of controlling ARF and RHD, best delivered through a register-based RHD control program; patients should be entered on an ARF registry, educated, and linked to follow-up before discharge (Harrison 22e p.2857-2858).
harrison.pathophysiology: ARF results from an autoimmune reaction to group A streptococcal infection, classically of the upper respiratory tract, with increasing evidence for a role of streptococcal skin infection. The most widely accepted theory is molecular mimicry: an immune response to streptococcal antigens (mainly the M protein) cross-reacts with human tissues. Antigen-presenting cells of the innate immune system present streptococcal antigens to T cells, activating humoral and cellular immunity; cross-reactive antibodies bind heart-valve endothelial cells, activating VCAM-1 with recruitment of activated lymphocytes and complement-mediated lysis, releasing peptides (laminin, keratin, tropomyosin) that activate cross-reactive T cells invading the heart, amplifying damage and causing epitope spreading. An alternative hypothesis proposes initial damage from streptococcal invasion of epithelial surfaces with M-protein binding to type IV collagen, rendering it immunogenic but not through molecular mimicry. Susceptibility is inherited (~3-6% of a population susceptible; 44% concordance in monozygotic vs 12% in dizygotic twins; heritability ~60%), with associations to HLA class II alleles, TNF and mannose-binding-lectin polymorphisms, the IGH locus (IGHV4-61*02), and complement factor H (Harrison 22e p.2854-2855).
additionalInvestigations: Always request: electrocardiogram (ECG), echocardiogram, complete blood count (CBC), C-reactive protein (CRP), and streptococcal serology (antistreptolysin O [ASO] and anti-DNase B [ADB]) (Harrison 22e p.2857).

Echocardiography should be performed on all possible cases to aid diagnosis (including detection of subclinical carditis/valvulitis) and to establish baseline carditis severity; auscultation is poorly sensitive and specific for RHD in asymptomatic patients (Harrison 22e p.2855, p.2857).

Because most cases lack a positive throat swab culture or rapid antigen test, serologic evidence of preceding group A strep infection is usually needed (ASO and anti-DNase B titers), ideally with locally derived age-specific reference ranges (Harrison 22e p.2856).

In relevant situations: throat swab, skin sore swab, blood cultures, synovial fluid aspirate (cell count, microscopy, culture, gonococcal PCR), pregnancy test, and creatinine/UEC (since NSAIDs can affect renal function) (Harrison 22e p.2857).

Tests to exclude alternative diagnoses (per clinical presentation/local endemic infections): autoantibodies, double-stranded DNA, anti-CCP antibodies; urine molecular testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis; serology for viral hepatitis, Yersinia, CMV, parvovirus B19, respiratory viruses, Ross River virus, Barmah Forest virus (Harrison 22e p.2857).

Inflammatory markers should be monitored every 1-2 weeks until normalized (usually within 4-6 weeks), and a repeat echocardiogram performed after 1 month to assess for progression of carditis (Harrison 22e p.2858).
redFlags: Severe carditis causing congestive heart failure; treatment of heart failure may be lifesaving (Harrison 22e p.2857).
Myocardial inflammation affecting conduction, causing P-R interval prolongation (first-degree AV block, rarely higher-level block) (Harrison 22e p.2855).
More than 50% of patients presenting with chorea have underlying carditis, mandating echocardiographic workup (Harrison 22e p.2856).
Advanced RHD complications: heart failure, arrhythmia, stroke, and infective endocarditis (Harrison 22e p.2856).
harrison.prognosis: Untreated, ARF lasts on average 12 weeks; with treatment, patients are usually discharged within 1-2 weeks. Almost all non-cardiac manifestations resolve completely. Inflammatory markers usually normalize within 4-6 weeks. Up to 75% of patients with ARF progress to RHD, the long-term consequence being valvular damage; people with RHD are often asymptomatic for many years before progression to cardiac failure. There is no treatment proven to alter the likelihood or severity of RHD; apart from heart-failure management, treatment of ARF is symptomatic. RHD is the most common cause of acquired heart disease in children in low- and middle-income countries and a major cause of adult mortality and morbidity, with >40 million people affected worldwide and >300,000 deaths annually (Harrison 22e p.2854, p.2857-2858).
pitfalls: The preceding group A streptococcal infection is commonly subclinical, so the absence of a reported sore throat or a negative throat swab/rapid antigen test does not exclude ARF; serologic confirmation is usually required (Harrison 22e p.2855-2856).

Diagnosis of ARF is often missed, particularly in resource-poor settings, so children, adolescents, and young adults may have undiagnosed RHD; echocardiographic screening can detect these cases (Harrison 22e p.2855).
Early commencement of anti-inflammatory medication before the typical migratory pattern is established may produce an atypical presenting picture such as aseptic monoarthritis (Harrison 22e p.2856).

Recurrence of fever, joint manifestations, and elevated acute-phase reactants up to 3 weeks after stopping anti-inflammatory medication does NOT indicate a true ARF recurrence and is managed by briefly recommencing anti-inflammatory agents (Harrison 22e p.2857).

Glucocorticoid use in ARF carditis remains controversial; two meta-analyses failed to demonstrate benefit over placebo or salicylates, though included studies were >40 years old and used outdated medications (Harrison 22e p.2857-2858).
Salicylates/NSAIDs are of no proven value in the treatment of carditis or chorea (they treat arthritis, arthralgia, and fever) (Harrison 22e p.2857).

Medications to control choreiform movements do NOT alter the duration or outcome of chorea; IVIg shows no benefit on short- or long-term carditis outcome and is not recommended except in severe chorea refractory to other treatments (Harrison 22e p.2858).
harrison.severityClassification: RHD detected by echocardiography is staged (2023 World Heart Federation guidelines) into: Stage A (minimal echocardiographic criteria for RHD, individuals aged <=20 years, mild MR or AR without morphologic features); Stage B (mild RHD, mild valvular regurgitation plus morphologic feature(s)); Stage C (advanced RHD at risk of clinical complications - moderate/severe MR or AR, any MS or AS, pulmonary hypertension, decreased LV systolic function); Stage D (advanced RHD with established clinical complications such as cardiac surgery, heart failure, arrhythmia, stroke, infective endocarditis). The 2015 revised Jones criteria additionally separate low-risk populations (ARF incidence <=2 per 100,000 school-age children, or all-age RHD prevalence <=1 per 1000) from moderate/high-risk populations, applying more sensitive criteria to the latter (Harrison 22e p.2856-2857).
management: Eradicate the precipitating group A streptococcus with penicillin, using benzathine penicillin injection or oral phenoxymethylpenicillin and a macrolide where penicillin-allergic
Treat arthritis and mild carditis with anti-inflammatory agents such as aspirin or naproxen, reserving corticosteroids for severe carditis
Manage rheumatic heart failure from valvulitis with diuretics and afterload reduction, and refer for valve repair or replacement in severe regurgitation
Treat Sydenham chorea symptomatically with rest and, when disabling, agents such as carbamazepine or sodium valproate
Institute long-term secondary prophylaxis with regular benzathine penicillin to prevent recurrent episodes and progression to rheumatic heart disease
Monitor with serial echocardiography and inflammatory markers to gauge carditis severity and confirm resolution
Refer to cardiology, enrol on a rheumatic heart disease register, and maintain dental hygiene with endocarditis precautions
